title: A comparative analysis of data preparation algorithms for customer churn prediction: A case study in the telecommunication industry
harvard_reference: Coussement, K., Lessmann, S. and Verstraeten, G. (2017) 'A comparative analysis of data preparation algorithms for customer churn prediction: a case study in the telecommunication industry', Decision Support Systems, 95, pp. 27-36. doi:10.1016/j.dss.2016.11.007.
abstract_summary: The paper treats data preparation as the step that converts categorical and continuous predictors into a form suitable for modelling, and asks how much the choice of preparation method matters for churn prediction. Using real cross-sectional customer data from a large European telecommunications provider, the authors tune a logistic regression (logit) model by comparing alternative data-preparation methods (citing papers name discretisation/binning and weight-of-evidence coding among them) and then benchmark this optimised logit against eight state-of-the-art data-mining techniques (including decision trees, neural networks, SVMs, naive Bayes and bagged/boosted trees) that use standard, unprepared inputs. Effective data preparation raised AUC by up to 14.5% and top-decile lift by up to 34%, and the well-prepared logit model was competitive with the more advanced single and ensemble classifiers. The authors conclude that practitioners' data-preparation choices genuinely affect churn-prediction performance.

claims_supported.claim: Data preparation choices (encoding, binning, transformation) significantly affect churn-model performance, and well-prepared logistic regression can rival more complex learners.
claims_supported.where: Abstract (and TL;DR/abstract summaries on Semantic Scholar and the UWA research repository): the study examines data-preparation alternatives for categorical and continuous variables to enhance a logit model; reports AUC improvements up to 14.5% and top-decile-lift improvements up to 34% from data preparation alone; and finds the optimised logit competitive with eight advanced single and ensemble data-mining techniques, concluding that the chosen data-preparation technique affects churn-prediction performance. Citing papers (Semantic Scholar citation contexts) confirm discretisation/binning and weight-of-evidence coding were among the techniques compared, and that the paper shows proper preprocessing makes logistic regression competitive with random forests, SVMs and other complex learners. Caveat: 'significantly' is supported in the sense of substantial effect sizes; the abstract does not state a statistical-significance test, so avoid implying one. The parenthetical 'encoding, binning, transformation' is a fair gloss of the categorical/continuous preparation methods, but the exact list of techniques should be checked against the full text before naming specific methods in the report.
